title: Rico Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Rico wells have a 110-foot median depth, with fractured-bedrock drilling commonly costing $13,200-$23,000 finished.
h1: Rico, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Rico sits in mountain terrain where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. The records near town show a 110-foot median well depth and a median reported yield of 10.5 gallons per minute, but the data is not complete: 67 wells are recorded as constructed, 76 report depth, 18 report pump yield, and only 6 report static water level.

That makes neighboring well records useful for planning, not a guarantee for a particular lot. A driller still has to evaluate access, rock, casing and grout requirements, the proposed use, and the chance that a fractured zone produces more or less water than nearby wells.

sections.heading: Rico well depths: shallow by mountain standards, but variable
sections.html:
Reported well depths around Rico have a 110-foot median, with the middle half between 64 and 143 feet. That is a useful starting point for a drilling estimate: a bid based near the median may be reasonable for a site with similar geology and access, but it should not be treated as a fixed target. The deepest recorded well is 400 feet, and the 90th percentile is 199 feet.

The depth mix shows why location matters. Forty-three percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 53% fall from 100 to 300 feet. Only 4% are from 300 to 600 feet, and none are recorded above 600 feet. Most permits name unnamed fractured bedrock rather than a consistent basin aquifer, so granite and gneiss structure can change quickly across a parcel.

sections.heading: Reported well yield near Rico
sections.html:
Among the limited number of wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.5 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.5 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Thirty-nine percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and another 39% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Twenty-two percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures describe reported tests, not a promise for a new hole. A yield around the median is generally useful for a household, but storage, pump sizing, recovery, and simultaneous use still matter. Ask for the original well construction and yield documents, not just a seller's verbal estimate. A domestic or household-use well also remains subject to its DWR permit terms.

sections.heading: Water levels and what the Rico records can show
sections.html:
The six wells reporting static water level have a median depth to water of 31 feet, with the middle half from 20 to 85 feet. That can help a contractor think about pump setting, trenching, and initial site planning, but the small reporting set is not enough to map a dependable water table across Rico.

The permit history does not provide a water-level series by decade, so these facts do not establish a dropping or rising trend. Water levels can vary with season, recharge, pumping and the local fracture network. Before buying, obtain the well permit, construction report and any available pumping or static-level measurements for the parcel and nearby wells. A current field measurement is more useful than assuming every lot shares the same water level.

sections.heading: Rico drilling history and the contractors in the record
sections.html:
Colorado DWR permit records include 125 wells within the mapped area, with 67 recorded as constructed. Permits span the 1970s through the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025. The largest permit group is from the 1990s, with 37 permits; the 2000s have 28, the 2010s have 20, and the 2020s have 17.

Mcpherson Drilling Co., also listed as Mcpherson, Billy G., appears most often with 20 records. Authorized, listed as Pe, Pg, appears with 13, and Bill Kissner Drilling Inc., listed as Kissner, Bill F., appears with 9. These names show local permit history, not current availability or a recommendation. Confirm licensing, insurance, references, access capability and the scope of any written bid before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new Rico well may cost
sections.html:
Rico's fractured mountain bedrock is the main cost variable. The drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 110-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $7,200 to $11,000. A finished well, including pump, tank, trenching and electrical, is estimated at $13,200 to $23,000.

That range is for planning, not a guaranteed contract price. A lot that needs difficult access, extra casing or grout, more drilling, special electrical work, or longer utility trenching can change the bid. Ask the driller to separate footage, casing, grout, mobilization, pump equipment, pressure tank, trenching, electrical work, testing and permits. Comparing bids is easier when every contractor prices the same scope and states what happens if the hole is dry or low-yield.

sections.heading: Rico risks to check before building
sections.html:
The local environmental map includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 220 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles. That does not prove contamination on a particular parcel, but it is a reason to check the exact location, drainage, historic uses and available water-quality records. Test the well water through a qualified laboratory after closing and again when conditions or occupants change.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured rock even when nearby wells perform well. Confirm the permit's allowed use, construction status, casing and grout details, and any required setbacks from septic components. A septic designer must evaluate soil, slope, groundwater and the proposed house location. Access for a rig, pump service and emergency repairs should be planned before finalizing a homesite.

sections.heading: Buying or building a lot near Rico
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit number and construction report, then compare nearby wells in Rico and the surrounding mountain communities. Look for consistent depth, yield and water-level information rather than relying on a single nearby success. The surrounding records include areas such as Ophir, Mountain Village, Telluride, Sawpit, Silverton and Placerville, but those places should be used only as broader context because fractured-bedrock conditions can change locally.

For a purchase, make well inspection, water testing, permit verification and satisfactory flow part of the contract. For a new build, have a driller review rig access and a septic professional review the site before committing to a house location. Keep an allowance for a deeper hole, storage or treatment if testing shows the lot needs it. The permit controls the legal use; it does not guarantee a particular yield.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Rico, Colorado?
faq.a: Rico wells in the available records have a 110-foot median depth. The middle half runs from 64 to 143 feet, while the deepest recorded well is 400 feet. Most reported wells are between 100 and 300 feet, but fractured granite and gneiss can produce different results across short distances.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Rico?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 110-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $7,200 to $11,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $13,200 to $23,000. Access, extra drilling and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Rico wells produce?
faq.a: Reported yields have a 10.5-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 5.5 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Thirty-nine percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 22% report 1 to 5. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute, though the yield data covers only 18 wells.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Rico?
faq.a: The records do not establish that every Rico well is safe to drink. The mapped area includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 220 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the specific well through a qualified laboratory, and review nearby historic mining and drainage conditions before relying on the water.

faq.q: Are Rico wells connected to a reliable water table?
faq.a: Only 6 wells report static water levels. Their median depth to water is 31 feet, with the middle half from 20 to 85 feet. That small sample cannot establish a town-wide water-table trend. Ask for the parcel's records and nearby measurements, and have a driller evaluate seasonal conditions and fractured-bedrock production.
